items.q: A 68‑year‑old man presents with sudden severe thoracic back pain at night, radiating to the left shoulder. X‑ray of the thoracic spine shows a lytic lesion at T8 with preserved disc space and a ‘winking owl’ sign. What is the most likely primary tumour?
items.e: The ‘winking owl’ sign (pedicle loss with intact disc) and a destructive lytic thoracic lesion in an older male point to lung cancer, the commonest thoracic spine metastasis.
items.note: Purely lytic, pedicle involvement with disc preservation is classic for lung metastasis.
items.reason: repeats cai20261118_022 (winking owl sign); primary ambiguous

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman with known breast cancer develops a pathological fracture of the right proximal femur. The lesion is mixed lytic‑sclerotic. Which drug is most appropriate to reduce the risk of further skeletal‑related events?
items.e: Bisphosphonates like zoledronic acid inhibit osteoclast‑mediated bone resorption and are standard for mixed breast metastases.
items.note: Bisphosphonates are evidence‑based therapy for bone metastases.

items.q: During work‑up of an unknown primary bone metastasis in a 72‑year‑old man, the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting focal marrow lesions is:
items.e: MRI of the whole spine is the most sensitive modality for detecting focal marrow infiltration, as it directly visualises marrow signal changes. Bone scan misses purely lytic lesions; PET‑CT is useful but not more sensitive for marrow disease, and CT is less sensitive.
items.note: Correct answer changed to MRI of the whole spine; the original marked answer (PET‑CT) is incorrect.

items.q: A 32‑year‑old woman presents with a slowly enlarging, painless mass in the distal femur. Plain radiographs show an osteolytic lesion with a soap‑bubble appearance. MRI with contrast is performed before any intervention. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
o: Perform a core needle biopsy at a tertiary sarcoma centre
items.e: Surgery must not precede staging; biopsy is the last step after imaging. The lesion’s imaging suggests a benign‑appearing cystic lesion, but definitive diagnosis requires a core needle biopsy at a sarcoma centre.

items.q: During a core needle biopsy of a pelvic mass suspected to be a sarcoma, the sample is sent for histopathology and cytogenetics. Which laboratory investigation is most likely to be requested to confirm a diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma?
o: Fluorescence in situ hybridisation for t(11;22)(q24;q12)
Next‑generation sequencing panel for metastatic cancers
items.e: Ewing sarcoma is characterised by the EWSR1‑FLI1 fusion translocation, best detected by FISH for t(11;22)(q24;q12).
items.reason: duplicate options; repeats ai20261118_157 (confirming EWSR1 fusion)

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man with a newly diagnosed osteosarcoma of the proximal tibia has an SUV of 9.8 on FDG PET‑CT. Which of the following statements best describes PET‑CT in the Staging of bone sarcomas?
o: It replaces bone scan for all patients
It is mainly used for high‑grade sarcomas and to assess chemotherapy response
It is inferior to CT chest for detecting lung metastases
It is only indicated when the lesion is less than 5 cm
items.e: FDG PET‑CT is increasingly used for high‑grade sarcomas (Ewing, rhabdomyosarcoma) and to evaluate treatment response, not to replace bone scan universally.

items.q: Which investigation would most accurately rule out skip lesions in a large diaphyseal Ewing sarcoma?
o: Whole‑body bone scan with Tc‑99m MDP
MRI of the involved bone with distal and proximal ends
items.e: MRI is the investigation of choice for local staging and can show skip lesions within the same bone, whereas bone scan may miss purely lytic lesions.

items.q: A 52‑year‑old man with type‑2 diabetes presents with a 3‑cm ulcer over the medial aspect of the right foot. Probe‑to‑bone test is positive and ESR is 85 mm h⁻¹. Which investigation is the most appropriate to confirm osteomyelitis?
items.e: MRI of the foot is the investigation of choice for suspected osteomyelitis in the foot – it detects marrow oedema and soft‑tissue changes early and with high accuracy. Plain films lag, CT is less sensitive for early marrow changes, and bone scintigraphy is non‑specific.
items.note: Answer was marked wrong; the correct answer is MRI
items.reason: repeats ai20261118_120 published today (diabetic foot MRI)

items.q: A 24‑year‑old sexually active man develops insidious mono‑arthritis of the knee with no previous trauma. Which organism is most likely responsible for the septic arthritis?
items.e: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the classic pathogen in sexually active young adults with acute septic arthritis.

items.q: Biofilm formation on dead bone or an intramedullary nail renders many antibiotics ineffective. Which drug retains activity against biofilm staphylococci and should always be used in combination?
items.e: Rifampicin penetrates biofilm‑enclosed staphylococci, but must be combined with another agent to prevent rapid resistance.

items.q: In sickle‑cell disease, osteomyelitis is most frequently caused by which of the following organisms?
items.e: Salmonella, especially S. enterica serovars, is the commonest pathogen in sickle‑cell osteomyelitis, although S. aureus remains frequent.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a pathological hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis?
items.e: Sequestrum, involucrum, and cloaca are characteristic of chronic osteomyelitis; diffuse marrow edema is an early, non‑specific feature seen in both acute and chronic forms.

items.q: A 22‑year‑old male presents with insidious knee pain, mild swelling and night sweats. X‑ray shows juxta‑articular osteoporosis and marginal erosions with a preserved joint space. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: The classic Phemister triad—juxta‑articular osteoporosis, marginal erosions and late joint space narrowing—points to tuberculous arthritis.
items.note: Phemister triad is pathognomonic for TB arthritis

items.q: Which investigation is recommended as the first diagnostic test for extrapulmonary tuberculosis in India?
items.e: CBNAAT (GeneXpert) detects MTB and rifampicin resistance within a few hours and is the WHO‐recommended first step in India.

items.q: A patient with suspected hip TB undergoes MRI. The scan shows a large, thin‑walled paraspinal abscess extending over three vertebrae with a relatively spared disc space. This appearance favours:
items.e: Tuberculosis forms large, well‑defined, thin‑walled abscesses that spread under the anterior longitudinal ligament; early disc sparing is typical.
items.reason: repeats b700 (TB vs pyogenic spondylitis on MRI)

items.q: In osteo‑articular TB, the joint space is usually
items.e: Mycobacteria lack proteolytic enzymes, so cartilage resorption is slow and joint space narrows late.
items.note: Cartilage destruction is slow in TB
items.reason: repeats ai20261118_053 (joint space preserved in TB)

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for developing osteo‑articular tuberculosis in India?
items.e: Recent flu vaccination has no established link to osteo‑articular TB; the others are well‑documented risk factors.

items.q: The earliest radiological sign of healing after antitubercular therapy in a vertebral TB lesion is:
o: Remineralization and sharpening of cortical margins
items.e: Repopulation of bone density and cortical refinement precede visible structural changes like joint space narrowing.
items.reason: repeats b940 (first radiological sign of healing)

items.q: An Indian patient with a hip swelling is found to have a positive Mantoux test and a history of contact with a TB patient. Which laboratory test would most directly confirm active disease in the joint?
items.e: GeneXpert on a synovial biopsy quickly detects MTB DNA and rifampicin resistance, directly confirming active joint TB.

items.q: A 14‑year‑old boy presents with bowing of the legs and a classic ‘rachitic rosary’. Blood work shows serum calcium 9.5 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L), phosphate 2.5 mg/dL (0.79 mmol/L), alkaline phosphatase 900 IU/L, 25‑hydroxyvitamin D 35 ng/mL, 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D 30 pg/mL and intact PTH 50 pg/mL. Which defect most likely explains his biochemical profile?
items.e: The profile shows normal calcium and low phosphate with inappropriately normal/low 1,25‑OH₂D and high alkaline phosphatase – classic phosphorus‑wasting rickets due to FGF23 excess from a PHEX mutation (XLH). The alternative defects would give normal phosphate or higher 1,25‑OH₂D, or affect calcium rather than phosphate.
items.note: Corrected biochemical values now align with XLH.

items.q:
Which laboratory abnormality is characteristic of hypophosphatasia rather than rickets?
A. Elevated alkaline phosphatase
B. Low serum calcium
C. Low serum alkaline phosphatase
D. High serum phosphorus
items.e: Hypophosphatasia is due to TNSALP deficiency; serum ALP is low, whereas rickets shows a rise in ALP.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with a T-score of –3.1 at the femoral neck and a recent vertebral compression fracture is being considered for anabolic therapy. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate first‑line choice for this patient?
items.e: Teriparatide is an anabolic agent that stimulates osteoblasts and is recommended as first‑line for patients at very high fracture risk (e.g., recent fragility fracture, T‑score ≤ –3.0). Antiresorptives alone are less suitable for such high risk.
items.note: All facts align with guidelines and Campbell’s notes.

items.q: A 72‑year‑old man on 5 mg IV zoledronate yearly reports flu‑like symptoms and myalgia after his first infusion. Which of the following measures is most likely to reduce the incidence of this reaction on subsequent infusions?
items.e: Paracetamol given before the infusion significantly decreases the acute phase reaction seen after zoledronate.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old woman has been on oral alendronate 70 mg weekly for five years. She now has a vitamin D level of 18 ng/ml and reports mild jaw pain after a dental extraction. What is the best next step?
o: Continue alendronate but start calcium 1200 mg/day
Stop alendronate and start zoledronate 5 mg IV
Continue alendronate, correct vitamin D, and arrange dental review
items.e: Correcting vitamin D, ensuring adequate calcium, and dental care address the low‑risk osteonecrosis of the jaw factor while maintaining antiresorptive therapy.

items.q: Which of the following statements best describes the bone‑remodelling target of denosumab?
items.e: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that neutralises RANKL, preventing it from binding to RANK on osteoclast precursors and thus inhibiting osteoclast formation.
items.note: Mechanism is unequivocally stated in the notes.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old postmenopausal woman with T‑score –2.6 and a normal FRAX hip risk score presents for treatment. Which of the following agents is the most appropriate first‑line choice based on current guideline thresholds?
items.e: Guidelines recommend an antiresorptive such as zoledronate for patients with T‑score ≤ –2.5 and no high‑risk features, making it the preferred first‑line over SERMs or anabolic agents.

items.q: After completing 3 years of IV zoledronate therapy, a patient’s BMD has stabilized at a T‑score of –2.8. According to ASBMR recommendations, what is the appropriate next step regarding bisphosphonate use?
o: Continue zoledronate yearly for 10 more years
Discontinue zoledronate and observe for 3 years before any intervention
items.e: After 3 years of IV bisphosphonate, a drug holiday of 2–3 years is advised if the patient is not high risk; stopping zoledronate is appropriate per ASBMR guidance.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old woman with chronic renal failure presents with sudden painful swelling of her right knee. Joint aspiration shows 12 000 WBC/mm³ and weakly positive, rhomboid crystals on polarized light. Which of the following is the most appropriate first‑line treatment for the acute phase?
items.e: In CKD, NSAIDs are often contraindicated and colchicine requires dose adjustment; low‑dose colchicine (0.6 mg twice daily) is safe and effective. The distractor high‑dose colchicine risks toxicity, and prednisone/naproxen are less appropriate.
items.note: Original answer incorrect; corrected to reflect renal considerations.

items.q: In a patient with chronic tophaceous gout, which of the following radiographic features is most characteristic of monosodium urate deposition?
o: Linear sclerosis of the distal radius
Articular cartilage loss with joint space obliteration
items.e: ‘Rat‑bite’ or Martel sign—punched‑out juxta‑articular erosions with sclerotic margins—is classic for gout.
items.note: Correct answer and explanation are consistent with Campbell.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old man presents with low‑grade back pain, a painless enlargement of the skull, and mild anterolateral bowing of the femur. Serum alkaline phosphatase is 850 IU/L (normal 30–120). Which imaging finding is most characteristic of the bone disease involved?
o: Cortical thinning and homogeneous sclerosis of the vertebral bodies (“ivory vertebra”)
Loss of subchondral bone in the femoral head
Coarse trabeculae with cortical thickening and a blunted “blade‑of‑grass” lytic front in the femoral diaphysis
A focal lytic lesion with a sclerotic margin in the proximal tibia
items.e: The description matches Paget disease. The classic imaging sign is coarse trabeculae with cortical thickening and a “blade‑of‑grass” lytic front in long bones.
items.note: All facts are consistent with Campbell’s definitions.

items.q: Which laboratory value is least useful for monitoring disease activity in a patient with extensive polyostotic Paget disease?
items.e: Serum calcium remains normal in Paget disease (unless immobilised). The other tests track bone turnover and are useful for monitoring.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman with long‑standing Paget disease of the pelvis develops new, severe, progressive hip pain and a widening of the femoral neck on X‑ray. Which complication is most likely?
o: Acute osteogenic sarcoma of the femur
items.e: In patients with extensive Polyostotic Paget, the most dreaded complication is a sarcoma (often osteosarcoma) presenting as new pain and soft‑tissue mass.

items.q: The most appropriate first‑line treatment for a symptomatic, medically fit patient with active pagetic bone disease is
items.e: Zoledronic acid is the preferred bisphosphonate for Paget disease, given as a single yearly infusion, and provides rapid pain relief and biochemical remission.
items.note: Matches the guideline and Campbell’s recommendations.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical site of Paget disease in the Indian population?
items.e: Hands and feet are rarely involved in Paget disease, even though the femur, tibia, and skull are common sites.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old man presents with insidious groin pain aggravated by weight‑bearing. Plain AP pelvis X‑ray is normal. MRI of the hip shows a T2 ‐ double‑line sign in the femoral head. Which statement regarding this condition is correct?
o: It is most likely osteonecrosis of the femoral head
The finding is diagnostic of early osteoarthritis
The lesion indicates a radial fracture of the femoral head
The double‑line sign is characteristic of bone metastasis
items.e: The T2 double‑line sign (high‑signal rim of granulation tissue next to a low‑signal sclerotic rim) is pathognomonic for osteonecrosis of the femoral head.
items.note: Fact is directly stated in the reference notes.

items.q: Which of the following investigations is most sensitive for detecting early, pre‑radiographic osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
items.e: MRI detects the characteristic signal changes long before radiographs or CT show any bone alteration, making it the investigation of choice.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old woman on chronic high‑dose oral prednisolone for lupus has recently developed bilateral groin pain. Which of the following is the highest risk factor for her developing osteonecrosis?
o: Total cumulative dose > 2 g prednisolone in 3 months
items.e: The ARCO 2019 criteria state that > 2 g prednisolone within 3 months is the threshold for steroid‑associated osteonecrosis risk.
items.note: Explicitly given in the ARCO criteria.

items.q: In a young male with sickle cell disease (HbSS), a hip X‑ray shows a well‑defined crescent shape radiolucent line. Which statement best describes this finding?
o: It represents a superimposed fracture caused by chronic steroid use
It is a subchondral collapse sign indicating impending femoral head collapse
It denotes early arthritis due to avascular damage
It is a normal variant in sickle cell disease
items.e: The crescent line on X‑ray is a subchondral fracture that marks the start of collapse in osteonecrosis.
items.note: Confirmed by radiographic description in the notes.

items.q: A 42‑year‑old man with a history of chronic alcohol abuse (≈350 mL pure ethanol/week for 8 months) presents with unilateral hip pain. Which of the following laboratory investigations is most likely to reveal a predisposition to osteonecrosis?
o: Coagulation profile for Factor VIII activity
items.e: Elevated lipoprotein(a) is a recognised thrombophilic risk factor that can predispose to osteonecrosis in alcohol‑associated cases.
items.note: Matches the reference list of coagulopathy risks.

items.q: Which is the investigation of choice for localizing the nidus of an osteoid osteoma in a patient with typical history of nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs?
items.e: Thin‑slice CT best delineates the <1.5 cm nidus and surrounding sclerosis, making it the gold standard for osteoid osteoma.
items.note: Consistent with Campbell’s and the reference notes.

items.q: An MRI of a patient with a presumptive osteosarcoma shows a large soft‑tissue component encasing the neurovascular bundle but no bone‑surrounding margin. Which surgical margin is most appropriate to minimise recurrence?
items.e: For high‑grade sarcomas like osteosarcoma a wide margin (normal tissue cuff) is the standard for limb‑sparing surgery.

items.q: A 23‑year‑old woman presents with a painless, well‑defined mass over the lateral side of her knee. Radiograph shows a cortical and medullary continuous outgrowth with a bell‑shaped cartilage cap. Which tumour is most likely?
items.e: Osteochondroma is the most common benign cartilage tumour. It shows cortical and medullary continuity with host bone, a cartilage cap and grows away from the joint.
items.note: Stem and answer match standard Olympus/Campbell orthopaedics facts.

items.q: What imaging feature on MRI best suggests malignant change in a solitary osteochondroma in an adult?
items.e: A cartilage cap thicker than 2 cm in an adult, irregularity or soft‑tissue nodularity raises suspicion for peripheral chondrosarcoma.
items.note: CT/ MRI criteria are well documented in Campbell.

items.q: In the WHO 2020 classification, which tumour is placed in the "intermediate (locally aggressive)" category?
items.e: ACT (formerly grade 1 chondrosarcoma of the appendicular skeleton) is considered locally aggressive and placed in the intermediate category.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old patient has a metaphyseal intramedullary lesion in the femur with punctate calcifications on X‑ray. A core biopsy shows hyaline cartilage without atypia. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Enchondroma is a benign intramedullary cartilage tumour that presents with punctate or “popcorn” calcifications.

items.q: Which molecular alteration is most frequently seen in primary chondrosarcomas of the central skeleton?
items.e: Around 50 % of conventional central chondrosarcomas harbour IDH1 or IDH2 mutations.
items.note: Molecular genetics table in Campbell and review notes.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with a tumour of the distal humerus that is eccentrically located in the metaphysis and shows a sclerotic border with stippled calcifications. Which tumour fits best?
items.e: Chondromyxoid fibroma is an intermediate, locally aggressive cartilage tumour that typically occurs in the metaphysis of long bones with a sclerotic margin.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with a painful, expansile lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, with a well‑defined sclerotic rim and no periosteal reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: The lesion is epiphyseal, has a sclerotic rim and located in a skeletally mature adult—classic features of a giant cell tumour.
items.note: Accurate, single‑best answer with plausible distractors.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old man has a 5‑cm lytic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis that shows a 'soap‑bubble' appearance and a geographic margin with no sclerotic rim. Which of the following is the preferred first‑line treatment?
o: Extended curettage with high‑speed burr and cement
items.e: Giant cell tumour with a Campanacci Grade II features is best treated with extended curettage plus adjuvants and cement to reduce recurrence.
items.note: Correct answer, other options clearly incorrect.

items.q: On MRI of a giant cell tumour, which characteristic finding is most suggestive of an aggressive secondary aneurysmal bone cyst component?
o: Diffuse low T1 signal with high T2 hyperintensity
Diffuse cortical thinning with no periosteal reaction
A central high T2 signal rim
items.e: Secondary ABC change produces fluid‑fluid levels and thick septa; this is a recognised aggressive feature.

items.q: After curettage of a Campanacci Grade III distal radius tumour, the surgeon chooses to fill the cavity with PMMA. Which of the following is an additional benefit of using cement?
o: Provides immediate structural support and creates a visible interface for early recurrence detection
Stimulates new bone growth within the cavity
Prevents future pathological fractures of the adjacent metacarpals
items.e: PMMA polymerisation is exothermic, killing residual tumour cells and its interface allows recurrence to be spotted on follow‑up imaging.

items.q: A 42‑year‑old man has a lytic lesion of the sacrum that breaches the posterior cortex and extends into the neural foramina. Which of the following is the preferred systemic therapy to reduce tumour burden before definitive surgery?
items.e: Denosumab targets the RANKL‑RANK pathway in neoplastic stromal cells, shrinking sacral GCT and reducing surgical morbidity.

items.q: On immunohistochemistry a tumour shows strong membranous positivity for CD99. Which of the following is the most characteristic differential for this finding?
items.e: CD99 is highly sensitive for Ewing sarcoma, though not perfectly specific.

items.q: Which chromosomal translocation is diagnostic of classic Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: t(11;22) is present in >90 % of Ewing sarcomas, forming the EWSR1‑FLI1 fusion.

items.q: Which investigation is the confirmatory test for an Ewing sarcoma demonstrated by a core‑needle biopsy?
items.e: Detection of an EWSR1 transgene (by FISH or RT‑PCR) is required to confirm Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: A 13‑year‑old adolescent with an expansile bone lesion has fever, anaemia and raised ESR. Which symptom pattern most strongly hints that the tumour is mimicking osteomyelitis?
o: Systemic features like fever and raised ESR
items.e: Ewing sarcoma may present with constitutional and inflammatory signs that resemble infection.

items.q: Which small‑round‑cell tumour can also show CD99 positivity but is not a true Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma may be CD99‑positive yet lacks the EWSR1‑FLI1 translocation.

items.q: In a bone small‑round‑cell tumour that is CD99‑positive and PAS‑positive, what feature would definitively exclude it being an Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: Small cell osteosarcoma produces osteoid; Ewing sarcoma does not.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a painless, 8 cm deep thigh mass that has grown over 6 months. MRI shows a heterogeneous, well‑marginated lesion with fat‑infiltrated septae, no necrosis, and a thickness of septa >2 mm. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.e: The thick, nodular septae (>2 mm) and non‑fatty areas in a deep lesion point to an atypical lipomatous tumour (a malignant, low‑grade liposarcoma).
items.note: Clear single best answer supported by imaging criteria.

items.q: Which imaging modality is the investigation of choice for local staging of a suspected soft‑tissue sarcoma?
items.e: MRI with gadolinium best evaluates tumour size, depth, compartment, neurovascular involvement and peritumoural oedema.

items.q: A core needle biopsy of a deep soft‑tissue tumour is performed through a small longitudinal incision in the limb. Which statement best describes the handling of the biopsy tract?
o: The tract can be left in situ as it is not contaminated
The tract should be excised en‑bloc with the definitive resection
The tract should be flushed with saline and closed
Only the nail bed should be removed
items.e: The biopsy tract is considered contaminated and must be excised with the tumour to avoid tumour seeding.

items.q: A 30‑year‑old presents with a slow‑growing, 6 cm thigh mass that is painless. The patient reports that it has been progressively enlarging for 3 years. Which red‑flag feature is present?
o: History of prior trauma, suggesting haematoma
items.e: A mass >5 cm is a red‑flag feature that warrants referral and imaging because malignancy risk is high.
items.note: Directly corresponds to established red‑flag criteria.

items.q: According to the FNCLCC grading system, a tumour shows the following: poorly differentiated cells (score 3), 15 mitoses per 10 HPF (score 2), and 60 % necrosis (score 2). What grade is assigned?
items.e: Total score = 3+2+2 = 7, which falls in the Grade 3 range (6‑8).
